q: The auditor performs a proof in total on payroll by taking prior year cost, adjusting for the average increment percentage and headcount movement, then comparing with actual. This is primarily:
o: A substantive analytical procedure over the payroll cost
A test of details on the individual employee pay records
A walkthrough of the payroll processing cycle end to end
A test of controls over the authorisation of payroll runs
why: Building an independent expectation from headcount and rate data and comparing it with recorded cost is a substantive analytical procedure. Its effectiveness depends on the reliability of the underlying headcount and rate data used to build the expectation.

q: Which procedure most directly detects ghost employees?
o: Recalculating the gross to net pay for a sample of employees
Matching the payroll master to HR records and bank details
Agreeing the payroll register total to the general ledger
Reviewing the authorisation of overtime hours by managers
why: Ghost employees exist on the payroll but not in reality, so cross checking against independent HR records and looking for duplicate bank accounts targets that specific risk. Recalculation and ledger agreement confirm accuracy of amounts paid to names already on the register.

q: Under Ind AS 19, the defined benefit gratuity obligation remeasurement comprising actuarial gains and losses is:
o: Deferred under the corridor approach over the average life
Recognised in profit or loss within employee benefit cost
Recognised in other comprehensive income, never recycled
Recognised in other comprehensive income, recycled later
why: Ind AS 19 requires remeasurements to go to OCI without subsequent reclassification to profit or loss, while current and past service cost and net interest go to profit or loss. The corridor approach was eliminated.

q: A leave encashment scheme allows accumulation and encashment on separation. Under Ind AS 19 this is classified and measured as:
o: A defined benefit plan with the remeasurements taken to OCI
A termination benefit recognised only on separation date
A short term benefit measured on an undiscounted basis
An other long term benefit with remeasurements in profit
why: Accumulating compensated absences payable beyond twelve months are other long term employee benefits requiring actuarial valuation, but unlike defined benefit plans the remeasurements go to profit or loss. Undiscounted treatment applies only where settlement is expected wholly within twelve months.

q: The auditor tests leavers. Which finding indicates the most serious control failure?
o: An employee who resigned in November was paid till March
Notice recovery computed on basic pay rather than gross pay
Exit interview documents missing for two of the leavers
Full and final settlement made two weeks after the exit
why: Continued payment after separation is a direct misappropriation or a serious completeness failure in the leaver deactivation control, causing an overstated expense. Delayed settlements and missing interview forms are process weaknesses with far lower financial consequence.

q: For statutory dues, the auditor finds employee provident fund contributions deducted in March were deposited in July. Under Ind AS and the Income Tax Act position for employee contributions, the deducted amount not deposited within the due date under the relevant statute is:
o: Allowable in the year of payment, whatever the due date
Disallowed permanently, as the statutory date was missed
Allowable if deposited before the return filing due date
Not an audit matter, being purely a tax computation issue
why: Employee contributions deducted from salary are governed by the specific deposit due date under the relevant labour statute, and delayed deposit results in disallowance that is not cured by payment before the return filing date. This is a reportable matter under CARO on statutory dues and affects the tax provision.

q: Which analytic best identifies payroll fraud through inflated overtime?
o: Agreeing the salary register to the bank payment file
Comparing the total payroll cost with budget at company level
Comparing overtime hours with attendance and feasible hours
Recomputing provident fund on a sample of pay records
why: Testing overtime against attendance data and physical feasibility isolates the specific manipulation, since fabricated hours often exceed available hours in the period. Company level budget comparison is too aggregated to reveal individual departmental abuse.

q: An auditor obtains the payroll bank transfer file and compares it to the payroll register. The number of credits exceeds the register headcount by four. This most likely indicates:
o: An error in the provident fund rate applied to the wages
Correct handling of employees who are on unpaid leave
A rounding difference arising in the net pay computation
Unauthorised payments made outside the payroll system
why: Payments made without a corresponding payroll register entry point to unauthorised disbursements or ghost credits, an occurrence and authorisation failure. Rounding and rate errors change amounts, not the number of payment instructions.

q: Under Ind AS 19, past service cost arising from a plan amendment is:
o: Recognised in profit or loss at the plan amendment date
Spread over the remaining vesting period of the benefits
Recognised in other comprehensive income as a remeasurement
Recognised only when the amended benefits actually vest
why: Ind AS 19 requires immediate recognition of past service cost in profit or loss at the earlier of when the plan amendment or curtailment occurs and when related restructuring costs or termination benefits are recognised. Deferral over the vesting period reflects the superseded treatment.

q: The auditor is testing the completeness of TDS on salaries. The most effective procedure is:
o: Agreeing the TDS challans to the entries in the bank statements
Reconciling salary cost with the taxable pay in the TDS return
Recomputing the tax deducted for the highest paid employee
Reviewing the appointment letters issued to the new joiners
why: A reconciliation between the books salary cost and amounts reported in the statutory return identifies salary components on which tax was not deducted. Challan agreement only verifies that what was computed was paid, not that everything taxable was captured.

q: A company grants a bonus that becomes payable only if the employee remains employed on 30 June following the year end. At 31 March, the correct treatment is:
o: Recognise the bonus only when it is paid to staff in June
Recognise the whole bonus, ignoring the future service condition
Accrue for service rendered, allowing for expected forfeitures
Disclose it as a contingent liability with no amount accrued
why: Employee benefits are recognised as services are rendered, but a genuine future service condition affects whether an obligation exists at the reporting date and requires estimating expected forfeitures. Blanket full accrual or pure cash basis both misstate the liability.

q: Which of the following is the strongest management control over payroll master data?
o: Monthly reconciliation of payroll cost to budget by the payroll head
An annual review of the salary structures by the committee
The processor may add employees but must retain the form
HR authorises master changes and the log is reviewed outside
why: Independent authorisation combined with review of a system generated change log by someone outside payroll prevents and detects unauthorised master data changes. Self-authorisation by the processor and high level budget comparison do not address individual record manipulation.

q: An actuarial valuation for gratuity uses a discount rate materially higher than yields on government securities of comparable maturity. The likely effect and audit response are:
o: Liability understated; challenge the rate against bond yields
No effect, since the discount rate changes only the disclosure
Liability understated, but an actuary cannot be challenged
Liability overstated; accept the rate as prudently chosen
why: A higher discount rate reduces the present value of the obligation, so an unsupported rate understates the liability. SA 500 requires the auditor to evaluate the competence, capability and objectivity of a management expert and the appropriateness of the assumptions used.

q: The auditor selects new joiners during the year and traces them to the payroll. This primarily tests:
o: Occurrence of the payroll expense recorded in the period
Completeness and accuracy of pay for the new employees
Existence of the gratuity liability at the reporting date
Classification between direct labour and indirect labour
why: Tracing from HR appointment records forward to the payroll tests that all genuine employees are captured at correct rates and dates, which is completeness and accuracy. Testing occurrence would run in the opposite direction, from the payroll to HR evidence.

q: A company capitalises payroll costs of an internal team into a self-constructed asset. The audit focus should be on:
o: Whether the employees signed the daily attendance register
Whether salaries were paid through the correct bank account
Whether the time is directly attributable, per time records
Whether provident fund was computed on the capitalised pay
why: Only directly attributable employee benefit costs arising from construction may be capitalised under Ind AS 16, with general administrative overheads excluded. The critical evidence is reliable time allocation records supporting the attribution.

q: The auditor recomputes ESI contributions and finds the company excluded contract labour engaged through an agency. The auditor should:
o: Restate payroll cost to include the agency invoices as pay
Treat the exclusion purely as a disclosure matter in notes
Accept it, since the agency is the employer in every situation
Assess principal employer liability and CARO reporting on it
why: The principal employer can carry liability for statutory dues of contract labour where the contractor defaults, creating a potential provision or contingent liability. This also feeds the CARO reporting on undisputed statutory dues outstanding.

q: Payroll cost as a percentage of revenue fell from 18 percent to 11 percent while headcount was stable. The most probable explanation warranting investigation is:
o: Payroll understated by omitted accruals or capitalisation
The gratuity liability was remeasured through OCI this year
Employees received a large increment during the same year
Revenue and payroll cost grew at exactly the same rate
why: A fall of this size with stable headcount points to payroll cost being removed from the profit and loss through unrecorded accruals or improper capitalisation, which must be tested. Equal growth in both would leave the ratio unchanged and increments would push it up.

q: In auditing a company that outsources payroll processing to a service organisation, the auditor should primarily:
o: Rely on the client view that the service provider is sound
Obtain a type 2 report and assess complementary controls
Audit the financial statements of the service organisation
Ignore the provider, as the client retains responsibility
why: SA 402 permits use of a type 2 report covering design and operating effectiveness of relevant controls, along with evaluation of whether the complementary user entity controls assumed by the report are actually operating. Client assurances are not audit evidence about the service organisation controls.
